c: What it does

A low-pass filter lets slow changes through and holds fast ones back. The simplest version uses two parts. The signal goes through a resistor, and a capacitor connects the far end of that resistor to ground. You take the output across the capacitor. A steady voltage passes untouched, because once the capacitor has charged, no current flows and nothing is lost in the resistor. A rapid ripple is flattened, because the capacitor cannot charge and discharge fast enough through the resistor to follow it. The same two parts sit on sensor inputs, audio tone controls and power rails everywhere.
Why it works

Think of it as a voltage divider in which the bottom leg changes with frequency. A capacitor resists slow signals strongly and fast signals weakly. Its opposition, called reactance, halves every time the frequency doubles. At low frequency the capacitor looks like a huge resistance, so nearly all of the input appears across it. At high frequency it looks like a small resistance, so most of the input is dropped across the resistor instead and little is left at the output. Nothing switches on or off. The filter simply slides from passing nearly everything to passing nearly nothing as the frequency climbs.
The cutoff frequency

The point where the slide begins in earnest is the cutoff frequency. It equals 1 divided by the product of 2, pi, the resistance in ohms and the capacitance in farads. Take 10 kilohms and 100 nanofarads. Multiply 10,000 by 0.0000001 and you get 0.001. Multiply by 6.28 and divide into 1, and the answer is about 159 hertz. At exactly that frequency the output is about 71 percent of the input, which engineers call the minus 3 decibel point. Half of the signal's power gets through. Well below 159 hertz, almost everything passes.
How steep it is

Above the cutoff, the output falls in a simple pattern. Each time the frequency goes up tenfold, the output drops to a tenth. With the 159 hertz filter, a tone at about 1,600 hertz comes out at roughly one tenth of its size, and one at 16,000 hertz at roughly one hundredth. That slope is described as 20 decibels per decade. It is gentle. A single resistor and capacitor will not separate two signals that are close together in frequency. It works well when the thing you want and the thing you do not want are far apart.
The same filter seen in time

Multiply the resistance by the capacitance and you get the time constant, in seconds. For 10 kilohms and 100 nanofarads it is 1 millisecond. If the input jumps suddenly from 0 to 5 volts, the output does not jump. It rises along a curve, reaching about 63 percent of the way, or 3.2 volts, after one time constant, and about 99 percent after five. This is the same behaviour as the frequency picture, described differently. A filter that blocks fast signals must also respond slowly to sudden steps. You always trade smoothness against speed.
The loading trap

The formula assumes that whatever feeds the filter has a low resistance and whatever follows it draws almost no current. Break that and the numbers move. Hang a 10 kilohm load on the output of the 10 kilohm filter and two things go wrong at once. The steady output falls to half, because the resistor and the load form a divider. The cutoff also doubles to about 318 hertz. A workable rule is to keep the load at least ten times larger than the filter resistor. When that is not possible, follow the filter with an op-amp wired as a buffer.
Putting it to work

Three jobs come up constantly. To turn a pulse-width signal from a microcontroller into a steady voltage, pick a cutoff far below the pulse rate. With pulses at 1,000 hertz, 10 kilohms and 1 microfarad give a cutoff near 16 hertz, which leaves only a small ripple. To quieten a noisy sensor before an analog input, set the cutoff a little above the fastest change you care about. And if you swap the two parts, with the capacitor in series and the resistor to ground, you get a high-pass filter with the same cutoff formula, which removes a steady offset and keeps the changes.
A clock in the brain

Nearly every process in your body follows a daily cycle: sleepiness, body temperature, hormone levels, digestion, even reaction time. The cycles are coordinated by a small cluster of nerve cells in the hypothalamus, deep in the brain, sitting just above the point where the nerves from the two eyes cross. This is the master clock. It keeps time by itself. People kept in constant dim conditions with no clues to the hour still sleep and wake on a regular cycle, which is why the rhythm is called circadian, meaning about a day.
It runs slightly slow

Left to itself, the human clock does not run at exactly 24 hours. Careful laboratory measurements put the average a little longer, at about 24 hours and 10 minutes, with variation from person to person. Without correction you would drift later every day. So the clock has to be reset daily, and the signal that resets it is light. Special cells in the retina, separate from the ones used for seeing shapes, report the overall brightness to the clock. They respond most strongly to blue light, which daylight is rich in.
Timing is everything

The same light does opposite things depending on when it arrives. Light in the hours after your usual waking time pulls the clock earlier, so that you feel sleepy sooner that night. Light in the evening and the first half of the night pushes the clock later. This is why bright screens and bright rooms late at night make it harder to fall asleep, and why a lie-in with the curtains shut lets the clock slide. Morning light is the most useful single tool for keeping the clock steady.
The evening signal

As your usual bedtime approaches, a gland in the brain releases melatonin, a hormone that tells the body night has begun. The rise starts roughly two hours before you normally fall asleep, provided the light is dim. Bright light suppresses it. Body temperature follows its own curve, falling through the night to a low point a couple of hours before your usual waking time. That low point is when alertness is at its worst, which is why the small hours of a night shift feel so hard.
Larks and owls

People differ in when their clocks are set, partly by inheritance. Some are naturally early and some late, and most fall in between. Age shifts it. In the teenage years the clock moves markedly later, which is biology and not laziness, and it drifts earlier again through adult life. Living against your own timing, for instance a late type who must rise at five for work and sleeps in at weekends, produces a mild and permanent jet lag. Keeping the same waking time all week reduces it.
Jet lag

After a long flight, your clock is still on home time, and it shifts by only about an hour a day. Travelling east is usually harder than travelling west. Going west asks you to stay up later, which the slightly slow clock is inclined to do anyway. Going east asks you to fall asleep earlier, against its drift. The remedy is timed light. After flying east, get outdoor light in the local morning and keep the evening dim. After flying west, get light in the local late afternoon and evening. Across eight or more time zones the right timing is less obvious, and a jet lag planner can work it out for your flights.
Daily practice

Four habits keep the clock in order. Get outside within an hour or so of waking, even on a grey day, since outdoor light is many times brighter than indoor light. Keep your waking time steady, weekends included. Dim the lights and screens in the last hour or two of the evening. And keep the bedroom dark. If you sleep badly for weeks despite this, feel sleepy in the daytime, or work shifts and are struggling, talk to a clinician, since sleep problems have many causes worth checking.
Doing nothing is a choice

Almost every decision comes with a default, the outcome that applies if you take no action. The plan your employer enrols you in, the settings a new phone ships with, the box already ticked on a form. In principle a default is only a starting point, and anyone can change it. In practice, large majorities never do. This is known as the default effect, and it is one of the most dependable findings in the study of decisions. It works on important matters as strongly as on trivial ones.
The organ donor figures

The best-known evidence comes from a 2003 paper by Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein, who compared European countries. In countries where people had to opt in to be organ donors, consent was low, about 12 percent in Germany. In countries where people were presumed to consent unless they opted out, it was over 99 percent, as in Austria next door. Two similar societies differed by a factor of eight on a serious question, and the difference tracked the form. Note that these are consent figures. Actual transplant rates depend on much else and differ far less.
Why defaults stick

Several forces push the same way. Changing a default takes effort, even if it is only finding the form, and effort postponed is often effort never made. A default also looks like a recommendation, as if someone who knows more has chosen it for people like you. And switching feels like taking responsibility. If you opt out and things go badly, the loss is your doing. If you stay and things go badly, it merely happened. People will accept a worse outcome to avoid that feeling.
Saving for retirement

Pension enrolment shows the effect on money. When American employers began enrolling new staff in retirement plans automatically, with the freedom to leave, participation among new employees rose sharply. An influential study by Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea, published in 2001, found it went from roughly a third to well over four fifths at one company. The same study showed the cost. Most people also stayed at the default contribution rate and the default fund, even when those were set low and cautious. The default helped them start and then held them back.
Defaults set against you

A default is chosen by someone, and that someone has interests. Free trials renew into paid subscriptions unless you cancel. Add-on insurance is ticked in advance at the checkout. Software arrives with data sharing switched on. Each relies on the fact that most people will not act. A useful habit is to treat any option that was selected for you as a proposal from the party who selected it, and to ask who benefits if you leave it alone.
Setting your own

The effect can be turned to your advantage, because you are allowed to set defaults for your future self. An automatic transfer to savings on payday makes saving the thing that happens when you do nothing. A standing weekly appointment for exercise does the same. So does keeping fruit on the counter and biscuits on a high shelf. In each case you make the decision once, when you are thinking clearly, and after that the path of least effort leads where you wanted to go.
An audit worth an hour

Once a year, list the defaults you are living with and never chose. Your pension contribution rate and fund. Your bank account and the interest it pays. Your insurance renewals, phone plan and subscriptions. The privacy settings on your accounts. For each, ask whether you would pick it today if you were starting fresh. Most will be fine. One or two will be costing real money, and changing them takes minutes. The effort that kept you from doing so was small. It was only larger than nothing.
Two labels

In the United States, loans and credit cards are advertised with an annual percentage rate, or APR. Savings accounts and certificates of deposit are advertised with an annual percentage yield, or APY. The difference is compounding. APR is the yearly rate before interest is charged on interest. APY is what you actually pay or earn over a year once compounding within the year is counted. For the same account, APY is always the larger number, unless interest is added only once a year, in which case the two are equal.
How the gap arises

Take a credit card with an APR of 18 percent, compounding monthly. The card does not charge 18 percent at the end of the year. It charges one twelfth of that, 1.5 percent, each month, on whatever is owed, including last month's interest. Carry 1,000 dollars for a year with no payments. After one month you owe 1,015. After two, 1,030 dollars and 23 cents, not 1,030. After twelve, about 1,195 dollars and 62 cents. The effective rate was 19.56 percent, not 18. That higher figure is the APY.
The conversion

To go from APR to APY, divide the APR by the number of compounding periods in a year, add 1, raise the result to the power of the number of periods, and subtract 1. For 18 percent monthly, that is 1.015 multiplied by itself 12 times, which gives 1.1956. For 24 percent monthly it gives 26.8 percent. The gap widens as rates rise. At 4 percent monthly the APY is 4.07 percent, a difference too small to notice. At credit card rates it is a point or two of extra cost.
Daily, monthly, yearly

Compounding more often raises the yield, but with sharply diminishing effect. At an APR of 18 percent, compounding once a year yields 18 percent. Monthly yields 19.56 percent. Daily yields 19.72 percent. Going from yearly to monthly added a point and a half. Going from monthly to daily added less than a fifth of a point. When a bank advertises daily compounding on savings as a selling point, it is true and nearly irrelevant. The rate itself matters far more than how often it is applied.
Why each side picks its label

A lender wants the cost to look low, so the headline is the APR. A bank taking deposits wants the reward to look high, so the headline is the APY. Neither is hiding anything, and American rules require these particular figures in these particular advertisements. The trap is comparing one against the other. A loan at 7 percent APR and a savings account at 7 percent APY are not paying and charging the same rate. Convert both to the same basis before you compare.
What APR leaves in and out

On mortgages and some other loans, the APR includes certain fees spread across the life of the loan, which is why a mortgage with a quoted interest rate of 6.5 percent might show an APR of 6.7 percent. That makes APR useful for comparing two loans with different fee structures. It has a weakness. The calculation assumes you keep the loan for its full term. If you sell or refinance after five years, upfront fees cost you more per year than the APR suggested.
Using it

Three habits follow. When borrowing, ask for the APR and the compounding period, and work out the yearly cost in dollars on the balance you expect to carry. When saving, compare APY with APY and ignore how often interest compounds. And when you carry a card balance, remember that the true yearly rate is above the number printed on the statement, which makes paying that balance down one of the most reliable uses of spare money. This describes how the figures work, and is not advice about any particular product.
What a set is

When you hold a pocket pair and one of the two remaining cards of that rank comes on the board, you have a set. It is three of a kind in its most disguised form, because two of the three cards are hidden in your hand. A player holding an ace and a king on a board of king, seven, deuce has no way to see that an opponent with pocket sevens is far ahead. Calling a raise with a small pair mainly in the hope of making this hand is known as set mining.
The number to remember

You will flop a set or better 11.8 percent of the time, which is about one flop in eight and a half, or odds of 7.5 to 1 against. The sum is short. Fifty unseen cards remain and two of them help you. The chance that all three flop cards miss is 48 over 50, times 47 over 49, times 46 over 48, which is 88.2 percent. If you could always see all five board cards the figure would rise to 19.2 percent, but you will rarely get to the river cheaply with an underpair.
Why 7.5 to 1 is not the price

It is tempting to conclude that you need 7.5 times the call in winnings to break even. In practice you need much more. Sometimes you flop the set and everyone folds to your first bet. Sometimes the opponent has missed and puts in nothing more. And now and then your set loses. A common working rule is that the player you are up against should have at least 15 times the size of the call left in their stack, and 20 times is more comfortable. The money you win must come from behind, not from the pot already there.
A worked example

The blinds are 2 and 5 dollars. A solid player raises to 15 and you hold a pair of fives on the button. The call is 15, so the rule asks for 225 to 300 dollars in the raiser's stack and in yours. If the raiser has 500, call. If the raiser has only 120 left, fold, since even winning the whole stack every time you hit would barely cover the seven or eight times you missed. The same reasoning says to fold small pairs to a large reraise. The price has tripled and the stacks have not.
How strong the set is

On a flop of king, seven, deuce in three different suits, a set of sevens has 91 percent equity against a pair of aces and 98 percent against an ace and a king that has paired the king. Draws change the picture. On king of spades, seven of spades, deuce of diamonds, an opponent with the ace and queen of spades still wins about 26 percent of the time. That is why a set should usually be bet at once on a board with two cards of a suit. Slow play gives the draw a free card.
When it goes wrong

Two fears come with sets, and one is mostly imaginary. When two players hold different pocket pairs, both flop a set only about 1 percent of the time. Losing set under set is painful and rare, and it is not a reason to fold a set of deuces. The realistic danger is the board itself: three or four cards to a flush or a straight by the river. Against that, your set has help. A flopped set improves to a full house or four of a kind by the river about one time in three.
Using it

Treat small pairs before the flop as a question about stacks, not cards. With deep stacks and a raiser who cannot fold an overpair, call and hope. With short stacks, or against a player who gives up easily after the flop, the same pair has little value as a call. When you miss, which is seven times in eight, let the hand go without a struggle unless you have a clear reason to continue. When you hit, build the pot from the first street. The profit from all those cheap folds arrives in a few large pots.
Before the box

Until the 1950s, general cargo crossed the sea as separate items: sacks, crates, barrels, bales, drums. Gangs of dockworkers carried each piece from a truck or railcar into a shed, then onto the quay, then into the hold, where it was fitted in by hand. At the other end the process ran in reverse. A ship could spend as long in port as at sea. Goods were damaged and stolen along the way. For many products, the cost of getting through the two ports was a larger obstacle to trade than the ocean in between.
One man's impatience

Malcom McLean ran a trucking company in North Carolina. He had watched his trucks wait at the docks while cargo was handled piece by piece, and he asked why the whole trailer body could not simply be lifted onto the ship. He sold his trucking business, bought a shipping line, and had a wartime tanker fitted with a deck to carry boxes. On April 26, 1956, the Ideal X sailed from Newark, New Jersey, for Houston with 58 containers aboard. A crane had loaded them in hours.
The numbers

The saving was dramatic. By figures widely cited from McLean's operation, loading loose cargo onto a ship at the time cost 5 dollars and 86 cents a ton. Loading the Ideal X cost under 16 cents a ton. The box was sealed at the factory and not opened until it reached the customer, so theft and breakage fell as well. A ship that could be emptied and refilled in a day earned money at sea instead of sitting at a quay, and that changed the economics of the vessel itself.
The standard

A box is only useful if every crane, ship, truck and railcar can handle it. Early containers came in many sizes, and each line's equipment fitted only its own. During the 1960s, international standards settled on lengths of 20 and 40 feet and on a common corner fitting, a design by the engineer Keith Tantlinger that lets a crane grab a box and lets boxes lock to each other in a stack. Capacity has been counted ever since in twenty-foot equivalent units. From then on, a container packed in one country could travel on any carrier.
Ports moved

Containers need deep water, vast paved yards and road and rail links, not rows of narrow piers and warehouses in a city centre. Old ports that could not adapt declined quickly. The piers of Manhattan and the docks of east London emptied, while new terminals grew at places such as Port Elizabeth in New Jersey and Felixstowe in England. Dock work changed from mass manual labour to a small number of skilled crane and vehicle operators. The disputes over that change were long and bitter.
What it did to trade

Once the cost of moving goods fell far enough, it became practical to make a product in several countries. Parts could be made where each was cheapest, shipped to another country for assembly and shipped again for sale. The supply chains behind electronics, clothing and cars depend on this. Ships grew to match. The Ideal X carried 58 boxes. The largest container ships built since the late 2010s carry more than 20,000 twenty-foot units, and a single vessel can hold the contents of thousands of trucks.
Why it is worth remembering

The container contained no new science. Steel boxes, cranes and ships all existed. The invention was a system: a standard unit and everything else redesigned around it. That is a useful pattern to recognise. Some of the largest gains come from agreeing on an interface, so that many separate parties can work together without negotiating each time. The cost was real too. It fell on dock communities, who lost a way of life within a generation.
