c: One question, two answers

A comparator has two inputs, marked plus and minus, and one output. When the plus input is at a higher voltage than the minus input, the output goes high. When it is lower, the output goes low. There is nothing in between. That turns a smoothly varying voltage, such as the reading from a light or temperature sensor, into a yes or a no. An op-amp with no feedback will behave this way, but a dedicated part such as the LM393 does it better. It is built to slam from one extreme to the other quickly and to recover at once.
The output needs a pull-up

The LM393 and many of its relatives have what is called an open-collector output. The chip can pull its output down to ground, but it cannot push it up. For the high state you add a resistor, commonly 10 kilohms, from the output to a positive supply. This looks like a nuisance and is in fact a feature. The pull-up resistor can go to a different supply from the one that powers the comparator. A comparator running on 12 volts can therefore drive a 3.3 volt microcontroller pin directly, simply by pulling up to 3.3 volts.
The chatter problem

Real signals carry noise, and slow signals spend a long time near the threshold. Put those together and a plain comparator misbehaves. Picture a light sensor switching on a lamp at dusk. As the light fades, the sensor voltage drifts slowly down through the threshold, and the noise riding on it crosses back and forth dozens of times. The output flips each time. A relay driven from it will buzz, and a microcontroller counting edges will count nonsense. The comparator is doing exactly what it was asked. The trouble is having a single threshold for both directions.
Hysteresis: two thresholds

The cure is to give the comparator two thresholds, one for a rising signal and a lower one for a falling signal. Once the output has switched, the signal must travel back across the gap before it switches again, so small noise cannot undo the decision. This is hysteresis. A room thermostat works the same way. It turns the heat on at 19 degrees and off at 21, not on and off at 20. You get hysteresis by feeding a little of the output back to the plus input through a resistor, so that the output state nudges its own threshold.
A worked example

Run the comparator from 5 volts. Two 10 kilohm resistors from 5 volts to ground set the plus input at 2.5 volts. Feed the signal into the minus input. Now add a 100 kilohm resistor from the output back to the plus input. When the output is high, that resistor pulls the plus input up a little, to about 2.6 volts. When the output is low, it pulls it down to about 2.4 volts. The signal must rise above 2.6 volts to switch the output low and fall below 2.4 volts to switch it back. The gap is about 0.2 volts.
Choosing the gap

Make the gap wider than the noise and no wider than the job can tolerate. Look at the signal on an oscilloscope, or log it, and see how much it jitters. If the noise is 50 millivolts from peak to peak, a gap of 100 to 200 millivolts gives a comfortable margin. Lowering the feedback resistor widens the gap. Raising it narrows the gap. Too wide and the circuit becomes sluggish, like a thermostat that lets the room swing by five degrees before it reacts. A filter capacitor on the signal helps as well, and the two cures work together.
Where you meet it

Comparators with hysteresis are everywhere once you look. A low-battery cut-off uses one so that the load does not flicker on and off as the battery recovers. Logic chips such as the 74HC14 build the idea into every input and call it a Schmitt trigger, which is why they clean up slow or noisy edges. Two practical cautions for the LM393. Its inputs work down to ground but not all the way up to the positive supply, so keep them about 1.5 volts below it. And tie the inputs of any unused half of the chip to fixed voltages so it does not chatter by itself.
What salt does to taste

Salt is one of the five basic tastes, and it also changes how you perceive the others. It suppresses bitterness, which is why a pinch improves coffee that has stewed, grapefruit and dark greens. With bitterness turned down, sweetness and aroma come forward. Food cooked without enough salt does not taste merely unsalted. It tastes flat, as though something were missing that you cannot name. The aim of seasoning is the point at which food tastes fully of itself, just short of tasting salty.
Salting meat ahead

Sprinkle salt on a piece of meat and watch. Within a few minutes, beads of moisture appear, drawn out by the salt. If you cook it now, that wet surface steams and browns poorly. Wait longer and something else happens. The salt dissolves into the moisture, and over the next half hour or more that brine is drawn back in, carrying salt below the surface. So there are two good moments to salt a steak or a chop. Either immediately before it goes in the pan, or at least 45 minutes ahead. A whole chicken benefits from a day, uncovered in the fridge.
Water for pasta and vegetables

Pasta and potatoes absorb water as they cook, and it is the only chance to season them all the way through. Salt added afterwards sits on the surface. A workable amount for pasta is about 10 grams of salt per litre of water, roughly two level teaspoons of fine salt. The water should taste pleasantly seasoned, like a mild soup. For green vegetables, well salted boiling water seasons them and helps them cook quickly enough to stay bright. Most of that salt goes down the drain with the water.
Drawing water out on purpose

The same pull that wets the surface of a steak is useful elsewhere. Toss sliced cucumber or shredded cabbage with salt and leave it for 20 minutes, then squeeze, and you get a salad or a slaw that stays crisp and does not flood the dressing. Salted aubergine slices give up water and absorb less oil when fried. Salting chopped tomatoes concentrates their flavour and gives you a seasoned juice to use in the dressing. In each case, rinse or reduce the salt elsewhere so the dish is not overdone.
A teaspoon is not a teaspoon

Salt varies greatly in how tightly it packs. Fine table salt is dense. Flaky kosher salt and sea salt flakes are light and full of air. A level teaspoon of table salt can contain nearly twice as much salt by weight as a teaspoon of some flaky salts. This is the commonest reason a recipe turns out too salty or too bland. Know which salt a recipe means, stick to one kind in your kitchen so your hand learns it, and for baking, brining and curing, weigh it.
Season in stages

Adding all the salt at the end gives a salty surface over a bland interior. Adding a little at each stage builds flavour through the dish. Salt the onions as they soften, which also draws out moisture and helps them cook evenly. Salt the meat before browning. Season the liquid when it goes in. Then taste and adjust at the end. Remember that liquids reduce. A stock that is correctly seasoned at the start will be too salty when boiled down by half, so season reductions late.
Fixing and judging

If a dish tastes dull, try a pinch of salt in a spoonful before adding it to the pot. If it tastes right but heavy, it may need acid, a squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar, and not more salt. If you have oversalted, dilute with more unsalted ingredients, since a potato dropped into the pot does little. Taste as you go, every time. People who have been advised by a clinician to limit salt should follow that advice, and acid, herbs and spices carry more of the load.
The missing half

Survivorship bias is the mistake of drawing conclusions from the cases that passed through some filter while forgetting those that did not. The survivors are visible and the failures are not, so the survivors look like the whole story. The classic case is the wartime study of bombers returning with bullet holes, in which the statistician Abraham Wald saw that the armour belonged where the returning planes were unmarked, since planes hit there had not come back. The same error appears in business, investing, health and everyday advice.
Lessons from the successful

Read a few profiles of company founders and patterns appear. They took big risks, ignored doubters, left university early, worked extreme hours. The trouble is that the same was true of a great many founders whose companies failed, and nobody wrote their profiles. A trait shared by all the winners tells you nothing unless you know how common it was among the losers. If 100 people take a wild risk and 3 succeed spectacularly, the 3 will credit the risk, and the 97 will not be asked.
Funds that vanish

Investing gives a measurable example. A fund company may launch many funds. Those that perform badly are closed or merged into others, and their records disappear from the tables. Look at the funds available today and their average past return is flattered, because the worst have been removed from the count. Any comparison of the funds that exist now against the market is biased upward for that reason. Careful studies add the dead funds back in, and the average result gets worse when they do.
They do not make them like they used to

Old buildings, old furniture and old tools often seem better made than modern ones. Some were. But what you are looking at is the fraction that lasted a century. The badly built houses of 1900 fell down or were demolished long ago, and the flimsy chairs were burned. The same filter applies to music and books. The songs still played from fifty years ago are the best few of that era, and they are being compared against everything released this year, good and bad.
When the filter is the result

The most dangerous version is when the selection process creates the very pattern you think you have discovered. Suppose a hospital studies its patients and finds that those who arrive by helicopter fare worse than those who arrive by car. The helicopter is not the cause. It is sent to the worst cases. Or suppose a coach studies athletes who reached the top and finds they all trained through injuries. Those who trained through injuries and were finished by them are no longer athletes and are not in the sample.
The question to ask

One question exposes the bias in almost every case. What would I be seeing if this did not work? If the failures would be invisible, then the successes you can see prove little. Ask where the sample came from and what had to happen for a case to be in it. Ask how many started. A testimonial page shows the customers who were happy. A list of long-lived people who smoked shows the ones who lived. In each case the denominator is missing.
Putting it to use

When you take advice from a success, look for people who did the same things and failed, and see what actually differed. When you judge a strategy, find the base rate: of all who tried it, how many got the result. When you review your own decisions, keep records of the ones that went badly as well as the ones that went well, since memory runs its own survivorship filter and keeps the wins. The aim is modest. Before you learn a lesson from what is in front of you, check what has been removed.
A small number on a large base

Investment funds charge an annual fee called the expense ratio, quoted as a percentage of everything you have invested. A fund charging 1 percent takes 1 dollar a year for every 100 you hold. It is taken quietly from the fund's assets, so you never see a bill. The reason it matters so much is that it is charged on the whole balance, every year, not on the year's gain. If a fund earns 7 percent before costs and charges 1 percent, a seventh of the return has gone.
The thirty-year sum

Put 10,000 dollars into an investment that grows 7 percent a year and leave it for 30 years. With no costs it becomes about 76,100 dollars. Now take 1 percent a year off the return, so it grows at 6 percent. After 30 years it is about 57,400 dollars. The difference is about 18,700 dollars, which is 24.5 percent of the larger figure. Nearly a quarter of the final sum went to fees, although no single year's fee looked like more than a rounding error.
Why it compounds against you

Each dollar paid in fees is also a dollar that stops growing. A fee paid in year one costs you that dollar plus thirty years of what it would have earned. That lost growth is the larger part of the damage. It is compound interest working in reverse, and it follows the same rule as the growth it removes. The longer the period, the worse the effect. Over 10 years, the 1 percent fee takes about 9 percent of the final sum. Over 30, a quarter. Over 40, close to a third.
The low-cost comparison

Run the same 10,000 dollars for 30 years at 7 percent, less a fee of five hundredths of a percent, which is the kind of charge some broad index funds make. It ends at about 75,100 dollars. The fee cost about 1,000 dollars across three decades, against 18,700 for the 1 percent fund. To justify the higher charge, a fund has to beat the cheaper one by nearly a full percentage point every year for 30 years, after its own costs. Some funds manage it for a while. Few have managed it for decades.
Fees you do not see in the expense ratio

The expense ratio is the main cost and not the only one. An adviser may charge a separate percentage of your assets each year, on top of the funds' own fees. Some funds carry a sales charge when you buy or sell, called a load. Funds that trade heavily incur dealing costs that reduce returns without appearing in the headline figure. In a taxable account, frequent trading can also create tax bills. Add the layers together. A 1 percent adviser fee on top of funds charging 0.75 percent is a 1.75 percent headwind.
What a fee should buy

Paying for something is not foolish. Good advice on how much to save, which accounts to use and how not to panic in a falling market can be worth a great deal, and some people would not invest at all without it. The useful question is what you receive for the money, and whether it could be bought another way, such as a flat fee for a plan. What rarely earns its keep is a high fee paid only for the selection of investments, since the fee is certain and the outperformance is not.
Finding your own number

Look up the expense ratio of each fund you hold. It is in the fund's fact sheet and on most account websites. Multiply each by the amount you hold and add them up to get your yearly cost in dollars. Add any advisory fee. Then ask what that sum buys. You cannot control what markets return. You can control what you pay, and the cost is one of the few figures about an investment that is known in advance. This is a way of thinking about costs, not a recommendation of any fund.
Start from the miss

Three cards arrive on the flop and you hold two. With two unpaired hole cards, you will pair at least one of them 32.4 percent of the time. Turn that around and you get the fact that shapes the game after the flop. An unpaired hand misses about two flops in three. That is true of an ace and a king just as it is of a seven and a deuce. The same applies to your opponent, which is why the player who bets first so often takes the pot.
Where 32.4 percent comes from

After your two cards, 50 remain. Six of them pair one of your cards and 44 do not. The number of possible flops is 19,600. The number made up entirely of cards that miss you is 13,244. Divide and you get 67.6 percent for a complete miss, so 32.4 percent for at least a pair. That figure includes the rare better results. Two pair using both your cards arrives about 2 percent of the time and three of a kind using one of your cards a little over 1 percent.
Suited cards

Two cards of the same suit flop a made flush 0.84 percent of the time, about once in 119 tries. They flop a flush draw, with two more of the suit, 10.9 percent of the time. From there the draw completes by the river about 35 percent of the time. Multiply through and a suited hand ends up making a flush by this route only a few times in a hundred. Being suited is worth a few percentage points of equity. It improves a hand that was already playable. It does not make a weak hand a strong one.
Connected cards

Take a jack and a ten. They flop a straight 1.3 percent of the time. They flop a draw with eight cards that complete it 9.7 percent of the time, and a gutshot with four such cards 16.8 percent of the time. So a strong straight draw is about as common as a flush draw, roughly one flop in ten. Cards with a gap between them make fewer straights, and cards near the ends of the deck, such as an ace and a king or a three and a deuce, make fewer still.
Overcards to your pair

Big pocket pairs fear one thing on the flop, a higher card. With two kings, an ace appears on the flop 22.6 percent of the time. With two queens, at least one ace or king appears 41.4 percent of the time. With two jacks, an overcard appears 57 percent of the time, more often than not. This is why jacks are awkward to play. They are a strong hand before the flop that will be looking at a higher card on most boards, and you should decide in advance how you will respond.
What the numbers say to do

Since everyone misses most flops, a bet represents a hand more often than it has one, and folding every time you miss is a costly habit against frequent bettors. Equally, a strong draw on the flop is uncommon enough that you should not pay over the odds before the flop hoping to find one. Choose starting hands because they make good pairs or dominate the hands that will call you. Treat flushes and straights as a bonus on top.
Carry four of them

Four numbers are worth keeping. You pair up on about one flop in three. You flop a flush draw with suited cards about one time in nine. You flop a set with a pocket pair about one time in eight and a half. And an overcard to two jacks shows up on more than half of flops. With those in your head, you can judge quickly whether an opponent's story is likely, and whether your own plan depends on an event that happens too rarely to pay for it.
The last Roman city

Constantinople was founded in the year 330 as the new capital of the Roman Empire. When the western half of the empire collapsed in the fifth century, the eastern half carried on, Greek-speaking and Christian, for another thousand years. Historians call it the Byzantine Empire. Its people called themselves Romans. By 1453 it had shrunk to little more than the city itself and a few scattered territories, surrounded by the growing Ottoman state. The city was still a great prize. It sat on the strait between Europe and Asia and controlled the passage to the Black Sea.
The walls

What had kept the city safe was its land wall, built in the fifth century under the emperor Theodosius the Second. An attacker met a wide moat, then a low wall, then an outer wall with towers, then a massive inner wall with taller towers. It ran for several miles from sea to sea across the neck of the peninsula. Sea walls guarded the other sides, and a great chain could be drawn across the mouth of the harbour, the Golden Horn. Armies had tried the walls for centuries and failed.
The two sides

The sultan, Mehmed the Second, was 21 years old. He brought an army usually estimated at 80,000 or more, and a fleet. Inside the walls, the emperor Constantine the Eleventh had about 7,000 fighting men to defend miles of fortification. Among them were several hundred soldiers from Genoa under Giovanni Giustiniani, an expert in siege defence. Appeals to the Christian powers of the west brought little. The siege began on April 6, 1453.
The guns

Gunpowder artillery was not new, but Mehmed used it on a new scale. A Hungarian gun founder named Orban, who had first offered his services to the emperor and been turned away for lack of money, cast enormous bronze cannon for the sultan. The largest fired stone balls weighing hundreds of pounds and could be fired only a few times a day. For weeks the guns battered the land walls. Each night the defenders filled the breaches with earth, timber and barrels. The old masonry had been built to stop ladders and siege towers.
Ships over the hill

The chain kept the Ottoman fleet out of the Golden Horn, so the sea wall along the harbour needed few guards. Mehmed removed that advantage with a feat of engineering. In late April his men built a track of greased timbers over the hill behind the suburb of Galata and hauled dozens of ships overland on rollers, launching them into the harbour behind the chain. The defenders, already too few, now had to spread along another stretch of wall.
The last assault

Before dawn on May 29, the Ottomans attacked along the whole land wall in waves. For hours the line held. Then Giustiniani was badly wounded and carried from the wall, his men wavered, and the sultan's elite troops, the janissaries, forced their way over the stockade. Constantine the Eleventh is said to have thrown off his imperial insignia and died fighting in the breach. His body was never certainly identified. By midday the city had fallen, after 53 days.
What changed

Mehmed made the city his capital and the great church of Hagia Sophia a mosque. The Ottoman Empire, now firmly astride two continents, would be a major power for more than four centuries. The Roman Empire, by one way of counting, had finally ended. The siege also carried a military message. High stone walls, the basis of defence for thousands of years, could be knocked down by cannon. Across Europe, fortress builders began replacing tall thin walls with low, thick, angled earthworks designed to absorb shot.
Three pins

The LM317 is a linear voltage regulator with three pins: input, output and adjust. National Semiconductor introduced it in the 1970s and several companies still make it. Fixed regulators give you one voltage per part number. This one gives any output from 1.25 volts to about 37 volts, set by two resistors, at up to 1.5 amps in the common package. It protects itself against overheating and short circuits, which is part of why it became the default choice for bench supplies and one-off projects. If you understand a single fact about how it behaves, you can design with it from memory.
The single rule

The chip adjusts its output until the output pin sits exactly 1.25 volts above the adjust pin. That is all. It does not know or care what the output voltage is relative to ground. Connect the adjust pin to ground and the output is 1.25 volts. Lift the adjust pin to 3.75 volts by any means and the output becomes 5 volts. The standard circuit lifts the adjust pin with two resistors, and it does so in a way that stays accurate as the load changes.
Setting the output

Put a resistor of 240 ohms between the output and adjust pins. Because the chip holds 1.25 volts across it, a fixed current of about 5 milliamps flows through it. That current has nowhere to go but down through a second resistor from the adjust pin to ground, and the voltage it develops there lifts the output. The output equals 1.25 volts times 1 plus the second resistor divided by the first. For 5 volts, the second resistor is 720 ohms. With 1.5 kilohms you get about 9 volts. A potentiometer in that position makes a variable supply.
Headroom

A linear regulator can only reduce voltage, and it needs some to work with. For the LM317, plan on the input being at least 3 volts above the output. A 5 volt output wants 8 volts or more coming in. If the input sags below that margin, the output follows it down and stops being regulated. This matters with batteries. A 9 volt battery feeding a 5 volt LM317 circuit starts with margin to spare and loses regulation well before the battery is actually empty. Regulators described as low dropout exist for exactly that situation.
The heat sum

Everything the regulator removes becomes heat. Multiply the voltage it drops by the current through it. With 12 volts in, 5 volts out and half an amp, it drops 7 volts and burns 3.5 watts. In the common tab package with no heatsink, each watt raises the chip's temperature by roughly 50 degrees Celsius, so 3.5 watts is far too much and the chip will shut itself down. A bare package is good for about 1 watt. Beyond that, bolt on a heatsink, and remember that the metal tab is connected to the output, not to ground.
A constant current source

The same rule makes a current regulator from one resistor. Connect the resistor between the output and adjust pins and take the load from the adjust end. The chip keeps 1.25 volts across the resistor, so the current is 1.25 divided by the resistance, whatever the load does. A 62 ohm resistor gives about 20 milliamps, enough to run a string of LEDs at steady brightness from a supply that wanders. For 1 amp you need 1.25 ohms, and that resistor dissipates 1.25 watts, so choose its power rating accordingly.
Building it properly

Three details separate a circuit that works from one that mostly works. Fit a capacitor of about 100 nanofarads close to the input pin if the supply is more than a few centimetres away, and about 1 microfarad on the output to steady it when the load changes suddenly. Keep the 240 ohm resistor close to the chip, since the regulator needs a small minimum load to stay in control and that resistor provides it. And pick a switching regulator when the voltage drop is large or the power comes from a battery, because a linear part wastes the difference as heat.
Proteins unfolding

An egg white is about nine tenths water, with proteins folded into tight bundles floating in it. Heat shakes those bundles until they unfold, and the loose strands then link to one another, forming a mesh that traps the water. That is the change from clear liquid to white solid. Keep heating and the mesh tightens and squeezes water out, which is why an overcooked egg is rubbery and a pan of overcooked scrambled eggs weeps. Cooking eggs well means stopping at the tender stage of that process.
Two parts, two temperatures

The white and the yolk contain different proteins that set at different temperatures. The white begins to thicken at about 62 degrees Celsius and becomes firm by about 80. The yolk begins to thicken at about 65 degrees and sets to a solid at about 70. Those few degrees are the whole game. An egg held at 63 degrees for a long time has a barely set white and a thick, liquid yolk. One taken to 75 has a firm yolk and a tender white.
Boiling is a race

In a pan of boiling water, heat travels from the outside in. The white, on the outside, reaches its setting temperature first, and the yolk at the centre lags behind. A soft-boiled egg is the moment when the white has set and the yolk has not caught up. For a large egg taken from the fridge and lowered into boiling water, that is about six minutes for a runny yolk, eight for a soft, jammy one and eleven or so for fully firm. Times vary with size and starting temperature, so test with one egg first.
The green ring

A grey-green layer around the yolk of a hard-boiled egg is a sign of overcooking. Prolonged heat releases sulphur from the white, and it reacts with iron in the yolk where the two meet. The compound is harmless. It comes with a dry, crumbly yolk and a sulphurous smell. To avoid it, cook the eggs no longer than needed and cool them at once in cold water, which stops the heat still travelling inwards and also makes them easier to handle.
Peeling

Very fresh eggs are hard to peel cleanly, because the white clings to the membrane inside the shell. As an egg ages over a week or two, it loses carbon dioxide through the shell and becomes less acidic, and the membrane lets go more readily. So eggs that have been in the fridge for a while are the better choice for boiling. Starting them in water that is already boiling, or steaming them, also tends to help. Crack the shell all over and peel under running water, starting from the wide end where the air pocket sits.
Scrambles and custards

Stirring eggs while they heat breaks the mesh into small curds as it forms. Low heat and patient stirring give small, creamy curds. High heat gives large, firm ones in seconds, and a moment too long gives dry ones. Take the pan off while the eggs still look slightly wet, since they carry on cooking. Adding milk, cream or sugar spreads the proteins further apart and raises the temperature at which they set. That is why a custard thickens at around 80 degrees and curdles if it boils.
Safety

Raw and lightly cooked eggs can carry salmonella, a cause of food poisoning. The risk from any one egg is small, and it is not zero. Mainstream guidance is that young children, pregnant women, older people and anyone with a weakened immune system should eat eggs cooked until both white and yolk are firm, or use pasteurised eggs for dishes that are not fully cooked. Keep eggs in the fridge where local guidance says to, and do not leave egg dishes sitting at room temperature for hours.
An old method

The method of loci, also called the memory palace, was taught to orators in ancient Greece and Rome, who had to deliver long speeches without notes. Cicero tells the story of its origin. The poet Simonides stepped outside a banquet hall shortly before the roof fell in, and afterwards he could name the dead by recalling where each guest had been sitting. The lesson drawn from it was that order and location hold memories in place. Competitors in modern memory contests still use the same method.
Why it works

Human memory was shaped by finding the way home and remembering where things are, not by storing lists of words. You can walk through your childhood home in your head and recall rooms you have not seen in decades. You probably cannot recall a shopping list from last week. The technique borrows the strong system to prop up the weak one. Each item you want to remember is turned into an image and placed at a spot along a familiar route. To recall, you walk the route in your mind and look.
Build the route

Choose a place you know thoroughly, such as your home. Fix a path through it and pick distinct stops in a set order: the front door, the coat hook, the hall table, the sofa, the television, the kitchen sink, the fridge. The stops must always come in the same sequence, because the sequence is what preserves the order of the list. Ten stops is plenty to begin with. Walk the path in your head twice, until you can name each stop without hesitation.
Place the images

Suppose the list is eggs, batteries, stamps, olive oil, a birthday card, onions and string. At the front door, picture a huge egg wedged in the frame, cracking as you push past. On the coat hook, a coat with batteries pouring from its pockets. The hall table is papered with stamps. The sofa is soaked in olive oil and you slide off it. The television is showing a giant birthday card singing. The sink is full of onions and your eyes sting. The fridge is tied shut with string.
Make them strange

Ordinary images fade and odd ones stay. The pictures that work are exaggerated, moving, and involve the senses: something enormous, something broken, a smell, a noise, something happening to you. Each image should interact with its location, not merely sit near it. An egg beside the door is forgettable. An egg jammed in the door that you have to break to get in is not. This takes a few seconds per item at first and becomes quick with practice.
What it is good for

The method suits anything with a fixed order or a set number of points: the headings of a talk, the steps of a procedure, a list of names, the main arguments of a chapter. For a speech, place one image for each section along the route and walk it as you speak. It is less suited to understanding. It holds the pegs and not the meaning, so use it once you already understand the material and need to keep it available. It combines well with spaced review.
Start tonight

Try it on tomorrow's to-do list. Use seven stops in your home and seven tasks. Spend ten seconds on each image, then walk the route once before bed and once in the morning. Most people recall all seven on the first attempt, and are surprised. Keep separate routes for separate purposes, such as your home for errands and your walk to work for a presentation, so that old images do not get in the way of new ones. Images you stop revisiting fade within days, and the route is free again.
The third statement

Companies publish three main statements. The income statement shows sales, costs and profit over a period. The balance sheet shows what the company owns and owes on one day. The cash flow statement explains how the cash balance moved between two balance sheets. It is the hardest of the three to dress up, because cash is either in the bank or it is not. It is divided into three sections, and reading them in order tells you most of what you need to know about how a business is really doing.
Operating: cash from the business itself

The first section starts with net profit and adjusts it back to cash. Costs that did not involve paying anyone this year, chiefly depreciation, are added back. Then come changes in working capital. If customers owe the company more than they did last year, that profit has not arrived as cash, so it is subtracted. If the company built up stock, the cash spent on it is subtracted too. If it is taking longer to pay suppliers, cash goes up. The total is cash from operations, the money the day-to-day business produced.
Investing: what was spent on the future

The second section records money spent on long-lived things and money received from selling them. The largest line is usually capital expenditure: buildings, machines, vehicles, software. Buying another company appears here as well. This section is normally negative, and that is healthy. A growing business has to invest. What matters is the relationship with the first section. A company that funds its investment out of operating cash is standing on its own feet. One that cannot is depending on outsiders.
Financing: dealings with owners and lenders

The third section shows money moving between the company and those who fund it. Borrowing brings cash in. Repaying debt sends it out. Issuing new shares brings cash in. Paying dividends and buying back shares send it out. A mature, profitable company usually shows a negative figure here, because it is returning money. A young company usually shows a positive one, because it is raising money. Neither is good or bad in isolation. It depends on whether the first section justifies it.
A worked example

A company reports a net profit of 10 million dollars. Depreciation was 4 million, so add it back. Customers owe 6 million more than a year ago, so subtract that. Stock rose by 3 million, so subtract that too. Cash from operations is 5 million, half the reported profit. It spent 7 million on equipment. It borrowed 4 million and paid 1 million in dividends. Add up 5, minus 7, plus 3, and cash rose by 1 million. This company is profitable on paper and is borrowing to pay for its growth and its dividend.
Free cash flow

One figure that does not appear on the statement is worth calculating. Take cash from operations and subtract capital expenditure. The result is free cash flow, the money left after the business has paid for itself and for the upkeep and expansion of its assets. It is what could be used to pay down debt, pay dividends or build up savings. In the example it is 5 million minus 7 million, or minus 2 million. A negative figure for a year or two during expansion is normal. Year after year, it has to be explained.
What to look for

Compare cash from operations with net profit over several years. They should move roughly together. Profit that consistently runs well ahead of cash is a warning that sales are being booked that customers have not paid for, or that stock is piling up. Check whether investment is paid for from operations or from borrowing. And look at where dividends come from. A dividend funded by free cash flow is sustainable. A dividend funded by new debt is a decision that will have to be revisited.
The situation

The action folds around to you on the button. Only the small blind and the big blind remain, each holding two random cards, and between them they have put 1.5 big blinds into the pot. A raise here is called a steal, though it is a perfectly normal play. You have the best position for the rest of the hand, only two players can stop you, and both of them will be out of position if they call. The question is how wide to raise, and arithmetic gives a good first answer.
The break-even point

Suppose you raise to 2.5 big blinds. You are risking 2.5 to win the 1.5 already there. If your cards had no value at all when called, the raise would break even when both blinds fold 2.5 times in every 4, which is 62.5 percent. Now make the raise 2 big blinds. You risk 2 to win 1.5, and the break-even point falls to 57 percent. A smaller raise needs to succeed less often. That is the main reason opening raises have shrunk over the years.
Two players have to fold

Both blinds must fold for the steal to win at once, so their individual folding frequencies multiply. If each folds 80 percent of the time, both fold 64 percent of the time, and the steal profits even with worthless cards. If each folds 70 percent, both fold only 49 percent, and worthless cards lose money. Watch the two players to your left for an orbit or two before you widen your range. One stubborn defender in the big blind changes the sum more than any chart does.
Your cards are not worthless

The break-even figure assumes you never win after being called, which is far too gloomy. When a blind calls, you still hold real cards, you act last on every street, and you will often win with a single bet on the flop. This is why the range of hands worth raising on the button is so wide. Hands like king and nine of different suits, or any two suited cards with some connection, fail as calls and succeed as steals, because part of their profit comes from the folds.
Antes change everything

In tournaments an ante is often added to the pot, commonly paid as one extra big blind. The pot before you act is then 2.5 big blinds, not 1.5. A raise to 2 big blinds now risks 2 to win 2.5 and needs to work only 44 percent of the time. That large shift is why late-stage tournament play looks so aggressive. The players raising with weak hands are not being reckless. The pot they are raising into has nearly doubled relative to the price of trying.
When to tighten up

The steal depends on folds, so its enemy is the reraise. If the players in the blinds reraise often, your weakest steals lose their raise without seeing a flop. Against them, drop the bottom of your range and keep hands that can call a reraise or raise again. Stack sizes matter too. When a blind has a short stack of 10 to 15 big blinds, expect an all-in over your raise, and only open hands you are content to call with, or hands so weak that folding to the shove is easy.
The view from the blinds

The same sum tells the blinds what to do. If a button raiser is opening very wide, folding the big blind 80 percent of the time hands over a steady profit. The big blind already has one big blind in the pot and is getting a good price to call, so it should defend with a wide range of suited and connected hands, and reraise some of the time with both strong hands and a few bluffs. The small blind has a worse price and worse position, and should mostly reraise or fold.
Warsaw

Maria Sklodowska was born in Warsaw on November 7, 1867, the youngest of five children of two teachers. Poland was then under Russian rule, and its universities did not admit women. She studied in secret with an informal network of classes that moved from house to house to avoid the authorities. She and her sister Bronislawa made a pact. Maria would work as a governess to pay for her sister's medical studies in Paris, and her sister would then help her in turn. She waited years for her chance.
Paris

In 1891, aged 24, she enrolled at the Sorbonne. She lived in an unheated attic, and by her own account sometimes had too little to eat. She took a degree in physics in 1893 and another in mathematics the following year. Looking for laboratory space, she was introduced to Pierre Curie, a physicist already known for his work on crystals and magnetism. They married in 1895. Their honeymoon was a cycling tour of the French countryside, on bicycles bought with a wedding gift.
A new property of matter

In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium gave off invisible rays that fogged photographic plates. Marie Curie chose these rays as the subject of her doctorate. Using a sensitive instrument Pierre had helped invent, she measured the faint electrical effect the rays produced in air. She found that the strength of the rays depended only on the amount of uranium present, not on its chemical form. She concluded that the rays came from within the atom itself, and she named the phenomenon radioactivity.
Two elements

She then noticed that pitchblende, a uranium ore, was more radioactive than its uranium content could explain. Something else had to be in it. Pierre put aside his own research to join her. In 1898 they announced two new elements: polonium, named for her homeland, and radium. To prove radium existed, they had to isolate it. Working in a draughty shed, she processed tonnes of ore by hand over nearly four years, stirring boiling vats with an iron rod, to obtain about a tenth of a gram of a radium salt.
Prizes and loss

In 1903 the Curies shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Becquerel. She was the first woman to win one. In 1906 Pierre was killed in a Paris street, struck by a horse-drawn wagon. She was left with two young daughters. The Sorbonne gave her his teaching post, making her its first woman professor. In 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, for the discovery of the two elements. No one else has won in two different sciences.
The war

When war came in 1914, she saw that X-rays could locate bullets and fractures before surgery, and that the army had almost no equipment near the front. She raised money, fitted cars with X-ray machines and generators, learned to drive, and took them to field hospitals herself. Her daughter Irene, still in her teens, worked beside her. She also trained women as X-ray operators. Well over a million wounded soldiers are estimated to have been examined with the units she organised.
The cost and the legacy

Nobody then understood the danger of radiation. She carried test tubes of radium in her pockets and kept them in a desk drawer, admiring their glow. She died on July 4, 1934, of aplastic anaemia, a failure of the bone marrow that was very probably caused by her years of exposure. Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes. A year after her death, her daughter Irene and son-in-law Frederic Joliot won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In 1995 her remains were moved to the Pantheon in Paris.
A resistor that feels heat

A thermistor is a small bead of ceramic whose resistance depends strongly on temperature. The common kind is called NTC, for negative temperature coefficient, which means the resistance falls as the part warms. They cost very little, respond in a second or two, and sit inside thermostats, battery packs, 3-D printers and car engines. The usual hobby part is rated 10 kilohms at 25 degrees Celsius. Two numbers on the datasheet describe it: that resistance at 25 degrees, and a figure called beta, often around 3,950, which says how steeply the resistance changes.
The curve is not a straight line

With a beta of 3,950, a 10 kilohm thermistor measures about 33.6 kilohms at freezing, 10 kilohms at 25 degrees and about 3.6 kilohms at 50 degrees. Near room temperature the resistance changes by roughly 4.5 percent for each degree. That is a very large signal. A platinum sensor changes by less than half a percent per degree. The price of that sensitivity is a curve. Equal steps in temperature do not give equal steps in resistance, so you cannot convert with a simple multiplication. The conversion takes a logarithm, which any microcontroller can do.
Wiring it

Make a voltage divider. Connect a fixed 10 kilohm resistor from the 3.3 volt supply to an analog input pin, and the thermistor from that pin to ground. At 25 degrees the two are equal and the pin sits at half the supply, 1.65 volts. At 50 degrees the thermistor has fallen to 3.6 kilohms and the pin reads about 0.87 volts. At freezing it reads about 2.54 volts. Choose the fixed resistor to equal the thermistor's resistance at the middle of the range you care about. That puts the steepest, most sensitive part of the response where you need it.
From a reading to a resistance

A 10-bit converter reports a number from 0 to 1,023, in proportion to the pin voltage. You do not need to turn that into volts. The thermistor's resistance equals the fixed resistor times the reading, divided by 1,023 minus the reading. Suppose the reading is 270. Then 270 divided by 753 is about 0.359, and the thermistor is 3.59 kilohms. The supply voltage cancelled out of the sum, as long as the converter uses that same supply as its reference. A sagging supply therefore does not disturb the temperature, which is a real advantage of the divider.
From a resistance to a temperature

The beta equation does the last step. Divide the measured resistance by the resistance at 25 degrees and take the natural logarithm. Divide that by beta. Add 1 divided by 298.15, which is 25 degrees expressed in kelvin. The result is 1 divided by the temperature in kelvin. For 3.59 kilohms the logarithm is about minus 1.026, and working it through gives 323.2 kelvin. Subtract 273.15 and you have 50 degrees Celsius. Over a span of a few tens of degrees this is good to a fraction of a degree. For wider ranges, datasheets give a three-term formula called Steinhart-Hart.
Where the errors come from

Three things limit accuracy. Tolerance comes first. A thermistor specified to 1 percent is good to about a quarter of a degree at 25 degrees, and the fixed resistor adds its own error, so use a 1 percent part there too. Self-heating is second. The measuring current warms the bead slightly. With 10 kilohms the power is a fraction of a milliwatt and the effect is small, but a low-value divider can add a visible offset. Resolution is third. Near 25 degrees a 10-bit converter resolves about a tenth of a degree. At the hot and cold extremes each count is worth much more.
When to choose something else

A thermistor suits the range from roughly minus 40 to 125 degrees Celsius, where it is cheap, fast and sensitive. For readings that need no arithmetic, a digital sensor such as the DS18B20 reports degrees directly over one wire, with a typical accuracy of half a degree. For ovens, kilns and flames, use a thermocouple, which survives many hundreds of degrees. For laboratory precision, use a platinum resistance sensor. Whichever you pick, check it against melting ice in water, which sits very close to 0 degrees, before trusting it.
How the tank works

A storage water heater is an insulated steel tank, typically holding 40 to 50 American gallons in a family house. Cold water enters through a tube that runs down inside to the bottom. Hot water, which rises, is drawn off from the top. A thermostat watches the temperature. When it drops, a gas burner under the tank or electric elements inside it switch on. Because the tank stays hot all day whether or not anyone uses it, some energy is always leaking away through the walls. That standing loss is the price of having hot water ready.
The relief valve

On the top or side of the tank is a brass valve with a small lever and a pipe running down towards the floor. This is the temperature and pressure relief valve, and it is the most important safety part in the house. Water heated in a sealed tank expands. If a thermostat failed and the burner stayed on, pressure would build until the tank burst. The valve opens before that can happen. Its discharge pipe must never be capped, plugged or blocked. If it drips or releases water, have a plumber find out why.
The anode rod

Steel and hot water make rust. The tank is lined with glass, but the lining always has small flaws. To protect the steel, a rod of magnesium or aluminium hangs inside the tank. That metal corrodes more readily than steel, so the corrosion attacks the rod and spares the tank. It is called a sacrificial anode, and it is used up over a period of years. Once it is gone, the tank itself starts to rust. Checking the rod every few years and replacing it when it is mostly eaten away can add years to a heater.
Sediment

Minerals dissolved in the water settle out when it is heated and collect at the bottom of the tank. In a gas heater the layer sits between the burner and the water, so the heater works harder and may rumble or pop as steam bubbles force their way through. In an electric heater it can bury and burn out the lower element. Draining a few gallons from the valve at the bottom once a year flushes much of it out. Hard water areas build sediment faster.
The temperature setting

The United States Department of Energy suggests a setting of 120 degrees Fahrenheit, about 49 Celsius, for most households. At that temperature a scald takes minutes of contact. At 140 Fahrenheit it takes seconds, which matters most for small children and older people. A lower setting also wastes less heat. There is a trade-off, since bacteria survive more easily in cooler stored water, and some households are advised to store hotter and mix cold in at the outlet. If someone in the home has a weakened immune system, ask a professional what is right.
Signs of trouble

Tank heaters commonly last somewhere around 8 to 12 years, less with hard water and no maintenance. Watch for rusty hot water, which suggests the tank is corroding. Watch for moisture or a rust trail at the base, and for hot water that runs out sooner than it used to. A tank that has begun to leak from its body cannot be repaired. Find the date of manufacture on the label, and if the heater is past ten years, plan for replacement before it fails on a cold morning.
What to do and what to leave

A homeowner can check the setting, look at the relief valve's pipe, drain sediment following the maker's instructions, and learn where the cold water shut-off and the gas or power shut-off are. Leave the rest to a licensed plumber: anything on a gas line or flue, replacing the relief valve, electrical work on the elements, and installing a new heater. If you ever smell gas, do not operate switches. Leave the building and call the gas company from outside.
The pattern

Any result that depends partly on skill and partly on luck will show the same behaviour. When the result is extreme, the next one tends to be closer to average. A golfer who shoots an outstanding first round usually scores worse in the second. A student with a terrible test usually does better next time. Nothing has to change for this to happen. The extreme result needed good or bad luck on top of ability, and luck does not repeat on demand. Francis Galton described the effect in the 1880s, while studying the heights of parents and children.
Why it must happen

Think of a score as ability plus luck. The people with the very best scores on a given day are, as a group, both able and lucky. Tomorrow their ability is unchanged, but their luck will be average on the whole, some up and some down. So the group's scores fall back part of the way towards the middle. The reverse holds for the worst scores. The more luck is involved in a result, the stronger the pull. Where there is no luck at all, there is no regression.
The instructor's mistake

Daniel Kahneman told of flight instructors who were certain that praise harmed performance and criticism improved it. They had seen it repeatedly. A cadet praised for an unusually good landing did worse the next time. A cadet shouted at for an unusually bad one did better. Both changes would have happened if the instructor had said nothing, because unusually good and unusually bad landings are followed by more typical ones. The instructors had drawn a firm lesson about teaching from a statistical effect.
Cures that do nothing

The same trap waits in health. People seek treatment when their symptoms are at their worst. Back pain, colds and low moods fluctuate, and the worst days are naturally followed by better ones. Whatever was tried at the low point, whether a remedy, a supplement or a change of pillow, gets the credit for an improvement that was coming anyway. This is the main reason medical research uses control groups. Comparing treated patients with similar untreated ones is the only way to separate the treatment from the drift back to normal.
Jinxes and slumps

Sport is full of supposed curses that are this effect in costume. An athlete appears on a magazine cover after the best run of their career, and the following months are less brilliant. A manager is sacked after a dreadful stretch, and results improve under the replacement. A rookie of the year has a weaker second season. In each case the moment of attention was chosen because of an extreme, and extremes are followed by something more ordinary whoever is on the cover or in the manager's chair.
In business and at home

A company's best-performing branch this quarter is unlikely to be the best next quarter. The sales representative who topped the table will probably do well, but less well. A speed camera placed at the site of last year's cluster of accidents will be followed by fewer accidents there, partly because a cluster is an extreme. Before you conclude that an intervention worked, or that a star has faded, ask what would have happened with no intervention at all.
How to allow for it

Three habits help. First, judge by long records, not by the latest result, since an average over many trials contains less luck. Second, when you predict what follows an extreme result, shade your guess towards the average, and shade it further when luck plays a larger part. Third, when testing whether something works, compare against a similar group that was left alone. And be slow to reward or punish on the strength of one outstanding or dreadful result. It told you less than it seemed to.
The product is a promise

An insurer sells a promise to pay if something bad happens. The customer pays first, in premiums, and the insurer pays later, in claims, sometimes years later and for most customers never. That order of events is unusual. Most businesses pay their costs first and collect from customers afterwards. An insurer collects first and learns what its product cost only when the claims come in. Its two sources of profit both follow from this: the margin between premiums and claims, and the use of the money in between.
Underwriting

Underwriting is the business of deciding whom to insure and what to charge. The insurer pools many customers whose individual losses cannot be predicted and whose combined losses can, within limits. Out of 10,000 similar houses, nobody knows which will burn, but the number that will is fairly steady from year to year. The premium has to cover the expected claims, the costs of running the company, and a margin. If the premiums collected exceed claims plus expenses, the insurer has made an underwriting profit.
The combined ratio

The industry measures underwriting with one figure. Add the claims paid and reserved to the expenses of running the business, and divide by the premiums earned. That is the combined ratio. Suppose an insurer earns 100 million dollars in premiums, incurs 70 million in claims and spends 28 million on staff, offices and commissions. The combined ratio is 98 percent, and the underwriting profit is 2 million. A ratio above 100 percent means the insurer paid out more than it took in on its policies.
Float

Between collecting a premium and paying a claim, the insurer holds the money. Added up across all policies, this pool is known as float. It does not belong to the insurer, since it is owed to future claimants, but the insurer invests it and keeps the income. An insurer with 100 million in annual premiums might hold 150 million in float. Invested mainly in bonds and earning 4 percent, that brings in 6 million a year, three times the underwriting profit in the example.
Why a small loss can be acceptable

Put the two sources together. An insurer with a combined ratio of 102 percent loses 2 million on underwriting, and with 6 million of investment income still earns 4 million overall. In effect it has borrowed 150 million at a cost of 2 million a year, cheaper than a loan. That is why lines of insurance where claims take years to settle, such as liability cover, attract so much competition. It is also the temptation of the business. Chasing float by cutting premiums too far turns cheap money into very expensive money.
What goes wrong

Three risks are built in. The first is mispricing, since premiums are set before costs are known, and an error is discovered only years later. The second is correlation. Houses in one town do not burn independently in a wildfire or flood in a hurricane, and a pool of risks that move together is not a pool. Insurers buy their own insurance, called reinsurance, to cap this. The third is investment loss on the float at the moment claims come due, which is why insurers are required to hold capital and invest mostly in safer assets.
Reading an insurer

To judge an insurance company, look at the combined ratio over ten years, not one, since a single year may be flattered by good weather. Look at whether reserves set aside for old claims have later needed topping up, which suggests past profits were overstated. And look at how the float has grown and what it earns. As a customer, the same picture explains your premium. You are paying for expected claims, the insurer's costs and its margin, less a little that its investment income lets it give back.
How often and why it matters

About 17 percent of flops, one in six, contain a pair. They play differently from other boards for one reason. With two cards of one rank already on the table, only two remain in the deck, so very few hands contain one. On a flop of king, seven, seven, most of the hands that either player can hold are no better than they were before the flop. Pots on paired boards are therefore often won by whoever shows interest first, and big hands are rarer than they feel.
Count the combinations

Put a raiser's likely hands on king, seven, seven and count. An ace with a king can be made 12 ways, since three kings and four aces remain. An ace with a seven of the same suit can be made only 2 ways. Pocket sevens, for four of a kind, 1 way. Even a player who calls with many suited hands containing a seven holds one a small fraction of the time. Hands with a king outnumber hands with a seven several times over in most ranges. Top pair is a strong hand here.
Who the board favours

The answer depends on the rank of the pair. On a high paired board such as king, king, four, the player who raised before the flop holds more kings, because raising ranges are full of high cards. On a low paired board such as five, five, deuce, the caller, particularly from the big blind, holds more fives, because cheap calls are made with small suited cards. When the pair is low and you were the raiser, expect more resistance. When the pair is high, expect to be given credit.
Betting as the raiser

Because the board is so hard to hit, a small bet does the work of a large one. A bet of a quarter to a third of the pot, made with most of your range, wins the pot often enough against hands that missed. It also keeps your losses small when you run into the rare three of a kind. There is little to protect against, since few draws exist on a flop like king, seven, seven in three suits, so large bets mostly fold out the hands you beat.
When you are raised

A raise on a paired board claims a narrow set of hands, mainly three of a kind. Since there are so few of those, a raise here is also a favourite bluff of aggressive players, who know you will rarely be strong either. Do not fold top pair automatically. Against a habitual bluffer, call and see what the turn brings. Against a quiet, careful player at low stakes, a raise followed by a second large bet on the turn is three of a kind far more often than not, and top pair becomes a fold.
Holding the three of a kind

When you do hold a seven on king, seven, seven, two things need watching. The first is your kicker. If an opponent also holds a seven, the side card decides the pot, and a seven with a small card is in poor shape against a seven with an ace. The second is the turn and river. Any king gives a full house to a player holding a king, which beats your three sevens unless you fill up too. Play the hand for value, and take pause if a passive opponent wakes up after the board changes.
A simple plan

As the raiser on a high paired board, bet small and often. As the raiser on a low paired board against a big blind caller, check more of your weak hands and be ready to be bet at. As the caller, pick a few hands with overcards or a possible draw and raise the small bet now and then, since the raiser is so often weak. And throughout, weigh a show of strength by the number of hands that could actually have it.
One face

Every human who has ever looked at the Moon has seen the same side of it. The familiar pattern of dark patches never rotates out of view. The far side stayed completely unknown until 1959, when the Soviet probe Luna 3 flew behind the Moon and sent back the first photographs. It is not a dark side. It receives as much sunlight as the near side does. When the Moon is new for us, the far side is in full daylight.
It does rotate

It is tempting to say the Moon does not spin. It does, once every 27.3 days, which is exactly the time it takes to circle the Earth. Try it with two objects on a table. Move a cup around a bottle while keeping the cup's handle pointed at the bottle. By the time the cup has gone all the way around, its handle has pointed in every direction of the room. It has turned once on its own axis. The Moon is doing the same thing.
How gravity did it

The match is the result of tides. The Earth pulls harder on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, which stretches the Moon very slightly into a rugby-ball shape with a bulge pointing towards us. Long ago the Moon spun faster. Its rotation kept carrying the bulge off the line between the two bodies, and Earth's gravity kept tugging the bulge back. That tug worked as a brake. Over millions of years it slowed the spin until the bulge stayed put, and the same face has pointed at Earth ever since.
A little more than half

Careful watchers can see slightly more than one hemisphere. The Moon's orbit is an ellipse, so it travels faster when near the Earth and slower when far, while its spin stays steady. The two get slightly out of step during each orbit, and the Moon appears to rock from side to side. Its axis is also tilted a little, which lets us peek over the top and bottom. These wobbles are called librations. Over time, about 59 percent of the surface can be seen from Earth.
The Earth is being braked too

The process runs both ways. The Moon raises tides in Earth's oceans, and the friction of that water against the sea floor slows our planet's rotation. The effect is tiny. The day lengthens by roughly 2 thousandths of a second each century. But it adds up. Growth lines in fossil corals suggest that about 400 million years ago a year held roughly 400 days, each a couple of hours shorter than now.
The Moon is leaving

The energy Earth loses goes partly into pushing the Moon outward. Apollo astronauts and Soviet rovers left reflectors on the surface, and observatories bounce laser pulses off them to time the round trip. The measurements show the Moon receding at about 3.8 centimetres a year, roughly the rate at which fingernails grow. In principle the process ends when Earth's day matches the Moon's orbit and each world shows the other one face. That would take far longer than the Sun will last.
A common arrangement

Tidal locking is the usual fate of a moon close to its planet. The large moons of Jupiter and Saturn all keep one face to their planets. Pluto and its moon Charon have gone the whole way and are locked to each other, so that from one side of Pluto, Charon hangs motionless in the sky and from the other side it is never seen. Many planets orbiting close to small, dim stars are expected to be locked as well, with one side in permanent day.
